scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): a recommendation response that argues unclear consequences describe most valuable research, then concedes caution where harm could be severe; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose at about 400 words on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: Almost every important discovery in history began as research whose final consequences nobody could clearly predict.
Some people recommend that governments should refuse to fund any scientific research whose consequences are unclear.
I understand the wish to avoid waste and danger, but I believe this recommendation would block most of the valuable research a society depends on.

sections.role: Body 1 — Why funding uncertain research is usually right

sentences.text: First, in the great majority of cases, unclear consequences are not a reason to refuse funding but the very nature of discovery.
When researchers explore something genuinely new, they cannot know in advance whether it will lead to a cure, a new material, or nothing at all.
For example, the early study of electricity seemed useless and unpredictable, yet it eventually came to power almost every part of modern life.
This shows that demanding clear consequences before funding would have stopped many of the breakthroughs we now take for granted.
A government that funds only safe, predictable projects will support little more than small improvements to things we already understand.
Real progress depends on accepting that most worthwhile research is uncertain at the very moment it begins.
For most science, then, unclear consequences are a normal cost rather than a good reason to withhold money.
Second, however, there are a few cases in which unclear consequences should genuinely make a government cautious.
If research could plausibly lead to serious and irreversible harm, simply not knowing the outcome is itself a warning.
Consider work on powerful new weapons or on altering the human genome, where a single mistake could affect millions of people permanently.
In situations like these, the lack of clarity is dangerous precisely because the possible damage is so enormous.
A wise government would fund such work only under strict supervision, or pause it until the risks are far better understood.
The problem in these cases is not uncertainty alone but uncertainty joined to the threat of catastrophe.
Here, caution about unclear consequences is reasonable and even necessary.
In conclusion, governments should not refuse funding simply because the consequences of research are unclear.
But they are right to be careful when uncertainty is combined with the risk of severe and lasting harm.
The sensible rule is to fund uncertain research freely while watching closely over the rare projects that could end in disaster.
